title: Non Overlapping Intervals
statement: You get a list of intervals. Remove as few as possible so that no two of the remaining ones overlap, and return how many you removed. Intervals that only touch, such as [1, 2] and [2, 3], do not count as overlapping here.

example.caption: Dropping [1,3] leaves [1,2], [2,3] and [3,4], which only touch. One removal is the minimum.

idea.sentence: Sort by end time and always keep the interval that finishes first: it leaves the most room for everything after it.

jargon.plain: Make the best-looking choice right now and never undo it. It works here because finishing earliest can never hurt later choices.
The end of the last interval we decided to keep. The next interval must start at or after it to be kept too.

watch.inputHint: One argument: a list of [start, end] pairs, e.g. [[1,2],[2,3],[3,4],[1,3]]

rows.name: Try every subset
rows.note: Check each subset for overlaps and keep the largest valid one.

rows.name: Greedy by end
rows.note: The sort dominates. The pass keeps one number: the end of the last kept interval.

fast.takeaway: Minimum removals equals n minus the largest set you can keep. Earliest finish builds that largest set.

stages.title: Sort by end
stages.note: Sort a copy by end. The first interval is always kept, and its end is the line to beat.

stages.title: Overlap test
stages.note: Does the next interval start at or after the kept end? Touching is allowed here.

stages.title: Keep it
stages.note: No overlap: keep it and move the line to its end.

stages.title: Remove it
stages.note: Overlap: remove this one. The kept interval ends no later, so it is the better one to keep.

stages.title: Return
stages.note: The count of removals is the answer.

edges.title: Touching is fine
edges.why: Each next start equals the previous end. The test is start >= keptEnd, so every one is kept.

edges.title: Empty list
edges.why: There is no first interval to keep. Return 0 before reading sorted[0].

edges.title: One long blocker
edges.why: Sorting by end drops only [1,6]. Sorting by start would keep it first and drop three.

edges.title: All identical
edges.why: Copies overlap each other, so keep one and remove the rest.

gotchas.text: Sort by end, not by start. Sorting by start and keeping the first interval can keep a huge one that blocks many small ones.
Touching is not overlapping in this problem: keep when start >= keptEnd. This is the opposite of merge-intervals, where touching merges.
sort() with no comparator compares as strings and changes the array in place. Copy first and pass (a, b) => a[1] - b[1].
sort.Slice reorders the caller's slice, because the outer slice shares memory. Copy it first with append([][]int(nil), intervals...).
sort.Slice is not stable. Equal ends may come out in any order. The answer is unchanged, but do not rely on the order of ties.

recap.key: Sort by end. Keep an interval if it starts at or after the last kept end. Count the ones you cannot keep.
recap.complexity: Time O(n log n). Space O(n).
moves: Keep the first and remember its end
If next start >= kept end, keep it and update the end
